title: Finnian and the Feathered Foe
markdown:
Finnian lived not in a grand towering castle but in a cozy cave tucked high on the windy Sunspike Peaks. A wizard, yes, but his spells sometimes took unexpected turns. One moment he’d be conjuring a sparkle, the next marveling at a fascinating beetle. He had the kindest eyes, the colour of warm honey, but they’d often drift away, watching dust motes dance or clouds float by.

This afternoon a very important job landed on his shoulders. He clutched a lantern. Light pulsed like a captured star, warm and steady. “Deliver this before moonset,” his mentor had said, voice like rustling leaves. “It lights the way for the night bloomers. They need your light.”

He nodded. Brow furrowed. He had to focus. Out he stepped, lantern careful in his hands. His scruffy raven, Scruffy, hopped beside him, every movement a comical flutter. Feathers ruffled by a gale and then forgotten, stuck out in all directions. Today Scruffy had a peculiar mission of his own. Anything with wheels. Anything that rolled. His arch-nemesis.

They were barely a minute from the cave, path still dusty from Finnian’s boots, when Scruffy stopped dead. Head cocked. A black comma against the blue sky. Beady eyes fixed. A wheelbarrow. Plain, wooden, leaning against an old gnarled oak. Perfectly ordinary. To Scruffy: a menace.

“Caw?” A very important question. Chest puffed. Tiny feathery dictator. He strutted closer, claws scratching dry earth, nudged it with his beak. Thump. The wheelbarrow wobbled, looking startled.

“Scruffy, no.” A familiar sigh. “We have to go. The Whispering Woods are this way.” Ancient trees close. Playful shadows even in daylight. Path dim and inviting.

Scruffy hopped in front of the wheelbarrow, a determined sentinel. Pecked at spokes. Tried to unravel its secrets. Glaring. “Caw. Caw.” A declaration of war. Clearly up to no good. A rival for Finnian’s affections, perhaps.

Finnian sighed. Sometimes the biggest challenge is not a fire-breathing dragon. It is a raven’s rivalry with a wood-thing. He tried to pull Scruffy away, tugged a ruffled wing feather. “Come on. It’s just a wheelbarrow. It can’t hurt you.”

Scruffy dug claws into dirt. Refused. Ruffled feathers dramatically. Furious caw. Pecked the wheel again. Tap, tap, tap. Honour. And Finnian’s, though he didn’t know it. Every peck cost minutes. Sun dipped, clouds orange and pink. Moonset approaching. The moon already a faint sliver, waiting.

“Right.” A tiny flutter of worry. “Focus.” Mentor’s words. Lantern steady, a miniature sun. Scruffy still squaring off as if the wheelbarrow were the greatest villain of all time. Deep breath. “Scruffy. Listen. This is important. More important than a silly wheelbarrow. The night bloomers are waiting.” He tried to sound stern. Voice wobbled a little.

A tiny puff of smoke drifted past his nose, faintly, delightfully, like toasted marshmallows. On a low-hanging branch, no bigger than his thumb, a dragon. Scales shimmered like a thousand tiny dewdrops.

“Hello?” Tinkling bells. “Are you all right? That raven is quite feisty with the wood-thing. He seems very cross.”

Finnian’s jaw dropped. “A dragon. And you can talk.” He’d read about tiny dragons. Never seen one.

The dragon puffed out its chest. A valiant little puffball. “I’m Puffkin. I can talk. And I can puff. See?” Another small puff of marshmallow-scented smoke, a tiny cloud curling playfully.

Scruffy heard the new voice, forgot the wheelbarrow a moment, hopped onto Finnian’s shoulder. Curiosity. “Caw?” Less aggressive. A questioning murmur.

Finnian lowered the lantern so Puffkin could look. “I need to get to the Whispering Woods. Deliver this lantern before the moon is too high.” Puffkin’s eyes widened at the gentle light.

“The night bloomers. They need the light to open. But your raven is very busy with that rolling thing.”

Scruffy, perhaps encouraged by the audience or the smell of toasted marshmallows, gave the wheelbarrow one last mighty peck. Not playful. Determined. A spoke snapped. The wheelbarrow tipped, spilled a pile of late-season berries onto the dusty path, red and purple like jewels.

“Oh, fiddlesticks.” Heart sank. Favourite snack for forest creatures. Time slipping.

Puffkin, seeing Finnian’s worried face and Scruffy’s bewildered look at the broken spoke, chirped, “Don’t worry. I can help. I might be small, but I have a very strong puff.”

He took a deep breath. Tiny chest like a miniature balloon. A gust of warm air, not smoke this time: a gentle focused breeze. Berries swept back into a neat pile. Then, surprising strength, a loose twig nudged into a tiny effective dam. The berries would not roll away.

“Wow.” A grin. “Thank you, Puffkin.”

Scruffy, berries tidied, duty to the wheelbarrow done for the moment, hopped off, a quick almost apologetic caw toward the broken spoke, a little flap as if to say: well, that’s that.

“Come on, Scruffy. Quickly. We’re almost there.”

With Puffkin fluttering beside them, a tiny beacon of helpfulness, they reached the edge of the Whispering Woods. Trees loomed, branches like ancient fingers. Path clear. Finnian held the lantern high. Glow seemed to welcome them into deepening shadows.

They hurried through the woods. The air grew cooler. Damp earth and pine needles. The moon was high now, a perfect sliver of silver in the inky sky, casting long dancing shadows. Finnian could see the glade where the night bloomers grew, petals tightly furled, waiting patiently for the moon’s gentle kiss. He ran the last few steps, boots silent on the soft moss, and placed the lantern gently on a mossy stone at the centre of the glade.

Instantly a soft ethereal light spread outwards, bathing the glade in a gentle radiance. The night bloomers, as if answering a silent call, began to unfurl their petals. They opened like pale moons. Delicate surfaces shimmered. The entire glade luminous. It was breathtaking.

Finnian beamed. His heart swelled. He’d done it. He’d delivered the lantern just in time. He looked down at Scruffy, preening, utterly unconcerned with the wheelbarrow, as if it had never happened. Puffkin landed on Finnian’s outstretched finger, tiny claws tickling.

“You did it,” Puffkin squeaked, full of joy.

Finnian smiled, warm and contented. “We did it. And you helped.” Scruffy gave a soft contented caw that sounded like all in a day’s work. The rivalry was, for now, a funny memory: a silly adventure that had almost caused a disaster and had ended with berries in a tidy pile and bloomers opening. Even if his raven had a strange fascination with moving objects, it was part of the adventure on the windy cliffs of Sunspike Peaks. The lantern stayed put, which was how you knew a wheelbarrow could lose a spoke and the woods could still bloom.
characters: Finnian (young wizard whose spells take unexpected turns), Scruffy (a raven who declares war on wheelbarrows)
